claims.text: The reported HfNbTiVAl10 state has a hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
The reported HfNbTiVAl10 state exhibits phase separation at multiple length scales.
A surrogate combining imaging-derived microstructural descriptors with reduced-order mechanical simulations can accurately predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness.
The proposed surrogate can overcome the high computational demands of first-principles and CALPHAD methods.
Standard analytical predictions cannot adequately account for microstructural defects in this material.
Phase-size distributions, interface-area fractions, and local-composition variance mediate load distribution in the hierarchical structure.
Phase-size distributions, interface-area fractions, and local-composition variance mediate flaw tolerance in the hierarchical structure.
Intrinsic microstructural heterogeneities influence local stress concentrations.
Defect-induced scattering and load partitioning strongly influence Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness.
A machine-learning model can map physics-informed microstructural descriptors to macroscopic mechanical responses.
The surrogate will be approximately 10 times faster than traditional first-principles and CALPHAD approaches.
The surrogate will reduce prediction error for Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness by 20–30% relative to traditional approaches.
Existing thermophysical, CALPHAD, and first-principles methods assume ideal defect-free crystals or provide only limited statistical representation of microstructural fluctuations.
The model should remain reliable when specimen microstructures fall within the distribution represented in its training data.
Unexpected phases, significantly altered interface chemistry, or microstructural scales outside the training regime may make the model unreliable.
Analogous high-entropy-alloy modeling successes provide a basis for the estimated 20–30% accuracy improvement.
The intended applicability domain is room-temperature to moderately elevated-temperature tensile and fracture testing matching prior characterization conditions.
A blinded prospective comparison will use imaging-derived predictions and tensile and fracture measurements from the same HfNbTiVAl10 specimens.
Prediction errors above a pre-established tolerance, exemplified as 30% relative error, will falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to achieve a near-10-fold computational speed improvement over traditional methods will falsify the hypothesis.
